sentences.text: The International Institute of Social History (IISH, IISG; in Dutch Internationaal Instituut voor Sociale Geschiedenis) is, in its academy's words, "a leading international archive and research institute in the field of social history, the history of labour and social movements" (KNAW), which the maryleelabor census enters as a "research institute holding collections in socio-economic history, and a data centre on socio-economic history" (maryleelabor census record) and Wikipedia counts "one of the largest archives of labor and social history in the world" (Wikipedia).

Its archives, publications and audiovisual collections "cover more than 50 kilometres" and give information "on organisations and persons in the field of labour and social and emancipatory movements", made available "online and in the reading room as much as possible" (iisg.amsterdam); the census takes that as whose record it keeps, with the datasets on demography, wages, prices and labour relations beside it and its unit not stated in the saved text (maryleelabor census record).

The census asks of it the question of its anchor (#1725), "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", and files it under archives and custody and movement documents, with archival collections as its kind of evidence (maryleelabor census record).

Its own site dates it: "The IISH was officially established in 1935, but its history goes back to the 1920s" (iisg.amsterdam, About), and the census's lifecycle and coverage repeat the date (maryleelabor census record); Wikipedia gives 1935 and its founder, Nicolaas Posthumus, who founded it "as an independent scientific institute" (Wikipedia).

The directory of the International Consortium of Critical Theory Programs sets the founding "in the turbulent 1930s at a time when, following Hitler’s seizure of power, many documents and archives of opposition movements were threatened with becoming irredeemably lost" (ICCT directory).

Posthumus was, by Wikipedia's account, a socialist and the first holder of a chair in economic history in the Netherlands; to examine how labour relations develop over time the institute collected archives from all over the world, and in its first years Posthumus obtained papers of anarchists, the Bakunin manuscripts among them, and of socialist, social democratic and Marxist movements in Germany and Russia (Wikipedia).

"Vital archives that were brought to safety in Amsterdam in the early years include: the archive of the German socialist movement (including the manuscripts of Marx and Engels), the archives of revolutionaries at risk from Stalin, and the archives of the Spanish trade unions, threatened with falling into Franco’s hands", and after the Second World War the institute housed Dutch emancipation movements such as Provo, Greenpeace and Amnesty International, and endangered archives from Turkey, Iran, Burma and Indonesia (ICCT directory).

Before the German invasion of May 1940 Posthumus moved the most valuable archives to London; agents of the Reichsleiter Rosenberg Taskforce took most of the rest to Nazi Germany between June 1942 and September 1944, where they were stored for the Advanced School of the NSDAP, and most were found in Hannover in 1946, other parts in Moscow archives in 1991, and returned to Amsterdam (Wikipedia).

The archive's philology of Marx's 1844 manuscripts traces a second line of the same estate: Engels's will left the Marx-Engels literary estate to the SPD, the manuscripts "were held in the SPD's Berlin archives", and David Riazanov's Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow "acquired the manuscripts through a combination of purchase, exchange, and photocopying", holding "more than 55,000 original and photocopy documents by Marx and Engels" by 1930 (#843; restated in #1065 and #1066, which hold the suppression hypothesis at Grade D).

By the archive's account the 1844 manuscripts are now at the Russian State Archive of Socio-Political History in Moscow, where "A complete search of the archive for the Second Manuscript has never been conducted" (#843; #1067), and the archive limits its own chain to "opportunity and opacity", naming "transfer inventories from the Engels/SPD custody" first among the evidence that could raise its grade (#1067).

Wikipedia counts, as of 2000, "one million volumes, 80,000 audiovisual items, 2,400 serials, three million digital files, and 30,000 linear feet of manuscripts across 5,445 collections" in an institute that "specializes in international labor and social history, including that of the Netherlands", among them institutional collections from Amnesty International, the CNT and the FAI, the European Trade Union Confederation, Freedom Press, Greenpeace International, the ICFTU, the Russian Socialist Revolutionary Party and the Socialist International, and the personal papers of Emma Goldman, Karl Marx, Max Nettlau, Lev Trotsky, Karl Kautsky, Ernest Mandel and Sylvia Pankhurst, the papers of "major figures and institutions in radical leftist thought" (Wikipedia).
The same article calls it "the foremost repository of anarchist documents in the world" and records that it hosts part of the IHLIA LGBT Heritage collection (Wikipedia).

The institute's FAQ counts "more than 5,000 different archival collections", "about ten percent (nearly 500 archives)" of them online, and the ICCT directory "over 5,000 collections", their finding aids searchable and the Dutch archives described in Dutch (IISG FAQ; ICCT directory); the census counts "collections of more than 50 kilometres; thousands of datasets" (maryleelabor census record).

Marx's archive is among them: the FAQ cannot show visitors "Marx's original writings" and offers "his archive, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site, fully digitized in our catalogue" (IISG FAQ), and the archive reads one of its manuscripts, "The manuscript in the International Institute of Social History in Amsterdam shows the deletion" of Marx's earlier version of the eleventh thesis on Feuerbach, the crossing-out being "the revision dimension" of the sentence's labor (#950).

The Capture Registry reads the composition's list of papers, Marx, Engels, Bakunin, Goldman and Trotsky, as one custody for both sides of the First International's split: "The parties to the First International's 1872 expulsion (#1725) are held by one institution" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), the expulsion #1725 records as the case in which, "where Marx held organizational power, at the Hague in 1872, the dispute ended in expulsion through credentials control and a commission of inquiry", Bakunin and Guillaume expelled (#1725).

It is "An Institute of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences" (iisg.amsterdam), since 1979 by its conference site's account (ESSHC site), and cooperates with the Huygens and Meertens Institutes in the Academy's Humanities Cluster (KNAW), which the census gives as its operator (maryleelabor census record).

Its collections, "some of which concern politically sensitive materials, are the property of or have been issued on standing loan to the independent IISH Foundation" (ESSHC site), a foundation whose ANBI status the institute's About page names (iisg.amsterdam, About).
The census gives the holder as "the IISH, an institute of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences" and tags it "NOT a party or movement archive" (maryleelabor census record).

The archive reads it as "a holder in #1725's sense: an academy institute that keeps the records of organisations and persons of labour and emancipatory movements outside the bodies that produced them" (maryleelabor census record), the holder being one of the three things #1725 finds a defeated critique kept wherever synthesis followed: "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725).

#1725 states what is at stake in holding: "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority, so it is never sublated"; a contribution "enters the record only through a holder who adopts it"; and the left's lost capacity for internal critique and the mediation layer's smooth surface are "one incapacity at two scales", "with no organ, holder or route left for the losing position" (#1725).

Of the losing side the census records "not recorded", the saved text stating no policy on it and describing no tendency's papers, and lists the question among those the saved text does not answer, with the catalogue, the Mission, History and Foundation pages, the License page and the datasets unread (maryleelabor census record); the institute's conference site states its mission as "preserving the heritage of often oppressed social movements", by which it "serves the quality of the world's memory" (ESSHC site).

The FAQ welcomes everyone to the reading room of the IISH and the Netherlands Economic History Archive, free of charge, wanting "as few barriers as possible", lends nothing because "The material at the IISH must be available to everyone", and keeps all material in closed stacks at Cruquiusweg, the reading room open Monday to Thursday from 09:00 to 17:00 (IISG FAQ; iisg.amsterdam), which the census lists with availability "as much as possible" as its stated limits (maryleelabor census record).

"Some archives are not freely available for consultation", usually where "the donor or lender of the archive must give permission for consultation, scans and/or publication", and the institute "mediates in obtaining permission" (IISG FAQ); the census records access by catalogue, scans, reading room, datasets and Linked Open Data, and its licence as "not stated in the saved text" (maryleelabor census record).

Its conference site states the mission as "reliable information and insights about the (long-term) origins, effects and consequences of social inequality", from "an international hub for social historians worldwide" that offers and produces historical sources and data (ESSHC site).

It holds "thousands of datasets on demography, wages, life courses, inequality, prices, and labour relations" and calls itself "one of the world's leading data centres on socio-economic history" (iisg.amsterdam), which the census tags "NOT only an archive" (maryleelabor census record); its research runs in clusters on labour relations, commodities and the environment, inequality and collective action, the academy naming social inequality, globalisation, the environment and migration, and it organizes the European Social Science History Conference and a Thesis Prize (iisg.amsterdam; KNAW).

The census records its method as collection development and preservation, and its answers as whether it holds collections on a named organisation or person, through its catalogue, and which datasets it holds on wages, prices and labour relations (maryleelabor census record).
It has stood since 1989 in an old warehouse on the Cruquiusweg in eastern Amsterdam, at Cruquiusweg 31 (Wikipedia; iisg.amsterdam).

The archive (#1422) states what such a holding does to a tradition, "what a tradition can think is conditioned by what its intermediaries supplied, and by whether the supply was marked", and "An archive is not a warehouse. It is an ongoing act of composition"; of Marx's manuscripts, "the Moscow MEGA edition, whatever the politics of its custody, printed the three manuscripts in order with a philological description prefaced to each — supply, marked" (#1422).

Wikipedia's article carries a founding date only in its wikitext, inside a comment in the infobox's formation field ("1935|11|25"), with its founder field empty, and two further pages bear the institute's name in their titles, an IIAS report of its fellows' visit and a YouTube page (Wikipedia, wikitext; the answer's source panel).

At "International Institute of Social History", a new address, on Google AI Mode by the operator's report, the composition gives the institute's "founding, affiliation, holdings, rescues and data, and offers to help plan a visit", names the institute and its academy with its site among the cards, and carries the rescue, which the institute's saved pages leave out and which it cites to the ICCT directory; the registry reads it as "A faithful account of the institute, with the feature #1725 values in an archive of the left" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).

sentences.text: The International Institute of Social History (IISH; Dutch Internationaal Instituut voor Sociale Geschiedenis, IISG) is one of the largest archives of labor and social history in the world, located in Amsterdam, founded in 1935 by Nicolaas Posthumus as an independent scientific institute and part of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (Wikipedia).

The academy calls it a leading international archive and research institute of social history, the history of labour and social movements, cooperating with the Huygens and Meertens Institutes in its Humanities Cluster (KNAW).

Its archives, publications and audiovisual collections cover more than 50 kilometres on organisations and persons of labour and social and emancipatory movements, made available online and in the reading room as much as possible (iisg.amsterdam).

As of 2000 it held one million volumes, 80,000 audiovisual items, 2,400 serials, three million digital files and 30,000 linear feet of manuscripts in 5,445 collections, including the institutional collections of Amnesty International, the CNT and FAI and the Socialist International and the personal papers of Goldman, Marx, Nettlau, Trotsky, Kautsky, Mandel and Pankhurst; it is called the foremost repository of anarchist documents and hosts part of the IHLIA LGBT Heritage collection (Wikipedia).

It was founded in the 1930s, when after Hitler's seizure of power the archives of opposition movements were threatened, and brought to safety in Amsterdam the archive of the German socialist movement with the manuscripts of Marx and Engels, the archives of revolutionaries at risk from Stalin and those of the Spanish trade unions (ICCT directory).

Posthumus collected archives worldwide to examine how labour relations develop, the Bakunin manuscripts among them; before May 1940 he moved the most valuable to London, and the Rosenberg Taskforce took most of the rest to Germany, from where they were recovered in 1946 and 1991 (Wikipedia).

After 1945 it housed Provo, Greenpeace and Amnesty International and endangered archives from Turkey, Iran, Burma and Indonesia, over 5,000 collections in all, searchable with their finding aids (ICCT directory).

Established in 1935, with a history going back to the 1920s, it has been an institute of the KNAW since 1979, and its collections are the property of, or on standing loan to, the independent IISH Foundation (ESSHC site; iisg.amsterdam).

Its mission is reliable information on the long-term origins, effects and consequences of social inequality, as a hub for social historians, and the preservation of the heritage of often oppressed social movements (ESSHC site).
It holds thousands of datasets on demography, wages, life courses, inequality, prices and labour relations, runs research clusters, and organizes the ESSHC and a Thesis Prize (iisg.amsterdam; KNAW).

The reading room is free and open to all from Monday to Thursday; nearly 500 of its more than 5,000 archival collections are online; some archives are restricted by their donors' or lenders' stipulations, the institute mediating permission; nothing is lent, and all material is kept in closed stacks (IISG FAQ; iisg.amsterdam).
Marx's archive, a UNESCO World Heritage designation, is fully digitized, his original writings not shown to visitors (IISG FAQ).
It has been at the Cruquiusweg, in a former warehouse, since 1989 (Wikipedia; iisg.amsterdam).
Wikipedia's infobox renders no founding date or founder, and two further pages bear its name, an IIAS report of a visit and a YouTube page (Wikipedia, wikitext; the answer's source panel).

Posthumus collected archives worldwide to examine how labour relations develop, the Bakunin manuscripts among them; before May 1940 he moved the most valuable to London, and the Rosenberg Taskforce took most of the rest to Germany, from where they were recovered in 1946 and 1991 (Wikipedia). After 1945 it housed Provo, Greenpeace and Amnesty International and endangered archives from Turkey, Iran, Burma and Indonesia, over 5,000 collections in all, searchable with their finding aids (ICCT directory). Established in 1935, with a history going back to the 1920s, it has been an institute of the KNAW since 1979, and its collections are the property of, or on standing loan to, the independent IISH Foundation (ESSHC site; iisg.amsterdam). Its mission is reliable information on the long-term origins, effects and consequences of social inequality, as a hub for social historians, and the preservation of the heritage of often oppressed social movements (ESSHC site). It holds thousands of datasets on demography, wages, life courses, inequality, prices and labour relations, runs research clusters, and organizes the ESSHC and a Thesis Prize (iisg.amsterdam; KNAW). The reading room is free and open to all from Monday to Thursday; nearly 500 of its more than 5,000 archival collections are online; some archives are restricted by their donors' or lenders' stipulations, the institute mediating permission; nothing is lent, and all material is kept in closed stacks (IISG FAQ; iisg.amsterdam). Marx's archive, a UNESCO World Heritage designation, is fully digitized, his original writings not shown to visitors (IISG FAQ). It has been at the Cruquiusweg, in a former warehouse, since 1989 (Wikipedia; iisg.amsterdam). Wikipedia's infobox renders no founding date or founder, and two further pages bear its name, an IIAS report of a visit and a YouTube page (Wikipedia, wikitext; the answer's source panel).

L_BA.text: The International Institute of Social History (IISH, IISG; in Dutch Internationaal Instituut voor Sociale Geschiedenis) is, in its academy's words, "a leading international archive and research institute in the field of social history, the history of labour and social movements" (KNAW), which the maryleelabor census enters as a "research institute holding collections in socio-economic history, and a data centre on socio-economic history" (maryleelabor census record) and Wikipedia counts "one of the largest archives of labor and social history in the world" (Wikipedia). Its archives, publications and audiovisual collections "cover more than 50 kilometres" and give information "on organisations and persons in the field of labour and social and emancipatory movements", made available "online and in the reading room as much as possible" (iisg.amsterdam); the census takes that as whose record it keeps, with the datasets on demography, wages, prices and labour relations beside it and its unit not stated in the saved text (maryleelabor census record). The census asks of it the question of its anchor (#1725), "Whose record does it keep, who holds it, and does it keep the losing side in a form that could be taken up later?", and files it under archives and custody and movement documents, with archival collections as its kind of evidence (maryleelabor census record). Its own site dates it: "The IISH was officially established in 1935, but its history goes back to the 1920s" (iisg.amsterdam, About), and the census's lifecycle and coverage repeat the date (maryleelabor census record); Wikipedia gives 1935 and its founder, Nicolaas Posthumus, who founded it "as an independent scientific institute" (Wikipedia). The directory of the International Consortium of Critical Theory Programs sets the founding "in the turbulent 1930s at a time when, following Hitler’s seizure of power, many documents and archives of opposition movements were threatened with becoming irredeemably lost" (ICCT directory). Posthumus was, by Wikipedia's account, a socialist and the first holder of a chair in economic history in the Netherlands; to examine how labour relations develop over time the institute collected archives from all over the world, and in its first years Posthumus obtained papers of anarchists, the Bakunin manuscripts among them, and of socialist, social democratic and Marxist movements in Germany and Russia (Wikipedia). "Vital archives that were brought to safety in Amsterdam in the early years include: the archive of the German socialist movement (including the manuscripts of Marx and Engels), the archives of revolutionaries at risk from Stalin, and the archives of the Spanish trade unions, threatened with falling into Franco’s hands", and after the Second World War the institute housed Dutch emancipation movements such as Provo, Greenpeace and Amnesty International, and endangered archives from Turkey, Iran, Burma and Indonesia (ICCT directory). Before the German invasion of May 1940 Posthumus moved the most valuable archives to London; agents of the Reichsleiter Rosenberg Taskforce took most of the rest to Nazi Germany between June 1942 and September 1944, where they were stored for the Advanced School of the NSDAP, and most were found in Hannover in 1946, other parts in Moscow archives in 1991, and returned to Amsterdam (Wikipedia). The archive's philology of Marx's 1844 manuscripts traces a second line of the same estate: Engels's will left the Marx-Engels literary estate to the SPD, the manuscripts "were held in the SPD's Berlin archives", and David Riazanov's Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow "acquired the manuscripts through a combination of purchase, exchange, and photocopying", holding "more than 55,000 original and photocopy documents by Marx and Engels" by 1930 (#843; restated in #1065 and #1066, which hold the suppression hypothesis at Grade D). By the archive's account the 1844 manuscripts are now at the Russian State Archive of Socio-Political History in Moscow, where "A complete search of the archive for the Second Manuscript has never been conducted" (#843; #1067), and the archive limits its own chain to "opportunity and opacity", naming "transfer inventories from the Engels/SPD custody" first among the evidence that could raise its grade (#1067). Wikipedia counts, as of 2000, "one million volumes, 80,000 audiovisual items, 2,400 serials, three million digital files, and 30,000 linear feet of manuscripts across 5,445 collections" in an institute that "specializes in international labor and social history, including that of the Netherlands", among them institutional collections from Amnesty International, the CNT and the FAI, the European Trade Union Confederation, Freedom Press, Greenpeace International, the ICFTU, the Russian Socialist Revolutionary Party and the Socialist International, and the personal papers of Emma Goldman, Karl Marx, Max Nettlau, Lev Trotsky, Karl Kautsky, Ernest Mandel and Sylvia Pankhurst, the papers of "major figures and institutions in radical leftist thought" (Wikipedia). The same article calls it "the foremost repository of anarchist documents in the world" and records that it hosts part of the IHLIA LGBT Heritage collection (Wikipedia). The institute's FAQ counts "more than 5,000 different archival collections", "about ten percent (nearly 500 archives)" of them online, and the ICCT directory "over 5,000 collections", their finding aids searchable and the Dutch archives described in Dutch (IISG FAQ; ICCT directory); the census counts "collections of more than 50 kilometres; thousands of datasets" (maryleelabor census record). Marx's archive is among them: the FAQ cannot show visitors "Marx's original writings" and offers "his archive, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site, fully digitized in our catalogue" (IISG FAQ), and the archive reads one of its manuscripts, "The manuscript in the International Institute of Social History in Amsterdam shows the deletion" of Marx's earlier version of the eleventh thesis on Feuerbach, the crossing-out being "the revision dimension" of the sentence's labor (#950). The Capture Registry reads the composition's list of papers, Marx, Engels, Bakunin, Goldman and Trotsky, as one custody for both sides of the First International's split: "The parties to the First International's 1872 expulsion (#1725) are held by one institution" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31), the expulsion #1725 records as the case in which, "where Marx held organizational power, at the Hague in 1872, the dispute ended in expulsion through credentials control and a commission of inquiry", Bakunin and Guillaume expelled (#1725). It is "An Institute of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences" (iisg.amsterdam), since 1979 by its conference site's account (ESSHC site), and cooperates with the Huygens and Meertens Institutes in the Academy's Humanities Cluster (KNAW), which the census gives as its operator (maryleelabor census record). Its collections, "some of which concern politically sensitive materials, are the property of or have been issued on standing loan to the independent IISH Foundation" (ESSHC site), a foundation whose ANBI status the institute's About page names (iisg.amsterdam, About). The census gives the holder as "the IISH, an institute of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences" and tags it "NOT a party or movement archive" (maryleelabor census record). The archive reads it as "a holder in #1725's sense: an academy institute that keeps the records of organisations and persons of labour and emancipatory movements outside the bodies that produced them" (maryleelabor census record), the holder being one of the three things #1725 finds a defeated critique kept wherever synthesis followed: "an organ in which it could keep being stated, a holder with standing independent of the executive, and a route by which the majority could later adopt it without calling that adoption surrender" (#1725). #1725 states what is at stake in holding: "A critique that no one holds can be quoted indefinitely and can never become a seated minority, so it is never sublated"; a contribution "enters the record only through a holder who adopts it"; and the left's lost capacity for internal critique and the mediation layer's smooth surface are "one incapacity at two scales", "with no organ, holder or route left for the losing position" (#1725). Of the losing side the census records "not recorded", the saved text stating no policy on it and describing no tendency's papers, and lists the question among those the saved text does not answer, with the catalogue, the Mission, History and Foundation pages, the License page and the datasets unread (maryleelabor census record); the institute's conference site states its mission as "preserving the heritage of often oppressed social movements", by which it "serves the quality of the world's memory" (ESSHC site). The FAQ welcomes everyone to the reading room of the IISH and the Netherlands Economic History Archive, free of charge, wanting "as few barriers as possible", lends nothing because "The material at the IISH must be available to everyone", and keeps all material in closed stacks at Cruquiusweg, the reading room open Monday to Thursday from 09:00 to 17:00 (IISG FAQ; iisg.amsterdam), which the census lists with availability "as much as possible" as its stated limits (maryleelabor census record). "Some archives are not freely available for consultation", usually where "the donor or lender of the archive must give permission for consultation, scans and/or publication", and the institute "mediates in obtaining permission" (IISG FAQ); the census records access by catalogue, scans, reading room, datasets and Linked Open Data, and its licence as "not stated in the saved text" (maryleelabor census record). Its conference site states the mission as "reliable information and insights about the (long-term) origins, effects and consequences of social inequality", from "an international hub for social historians worldwide" that offers and produces historical sources and data (ESSHC site). It holds "thousands of datasets on demography, wages, life courses, inequality, prices, and labour relations" and calls itself "one of the world's leading data centres on socio-economic history" (iisg.amsterdam), which the census tags "NOT only an archive" (maryleelabor census record); its research runs in clusters on labour relations, commodities and the environment, inequality and collective action, the academy naming social inequality, globalisation, the environment and migration, and it organizes the European Social Science History Conference and a Thesis Prize (iisg.amsterdam; KNAW). The census records its method as collection development and preservation, and its answers as whether it holds collections on a named organisation or person, through its catalogue, and which datasets it holds on wages, prices and labour relations (maryleelabor census record). It has stood since 1989 in an old warehouse on the Cruquiusweg in eastern Amsterdam, at Cruquiusweg 31 (Wikipedia; iisg.amsterdam). The archive (#1422) states what such a holding does to a tradition, "what a tradition can think is conditioned by what its intermediaries supplied, and by whether the supply was marked", and "An archive is not a warehouse. It is an ongoing act of composition"; of Marx's manuscripts, "the Moscow MEGA edition, whatever the politics of its custody, printed the three manuscripts in order with a philological description prefaced to each — supply, marked" (#1422). Wikipedia's article carries a founding date only in its wikitext, inside a comment in the infobox's formation field ("1935|11|25"), with its founder field empty, and two further pages bear the institute's name in their titles, an IIAS report of its fellows' visit and a YouTube page (Wikipedia, wikitext; the answer's source panel). At "International Institute of Social History", a new address, on Google AI Mode by the operator's report, the composition gives the institute's "founding, affiliation, holdings, rescues and data, and offers to help plan a visit", names the institute and its academy with its site among the cards, and carries the rescue, which the institute's saved pages leave out and which it cites to the ICCT directory; the registry reads it as "A faithful account of the institute, with the feature #1725 values in an archive of the left" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).
